findings.title: Router invariant handler can discard invalid-metadata acceptance evidence
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The payBadMetadata handler reverts from its successful external-call branch when the router accepts invalid metadata. The invariant configuration sets fail_on_revert=false. That handler revert rolls back the successful router operation and can be discarded by the invariant campaign; it leaves no persistent acceptance flag for an invariant to inspect. This weakens this stateful property. Separate router unit and fuzz tests still cover metadata rejection, and no production acceptance defect was established.
findings.impact_preconditions: A future regression accepts the malformed metadata exercised by this handler, and the campaign uses the checked-in invariant configuration. The finding concerns verification assurance, not an established current fund-loss path.
findings.remediation: Record unexpected acceptance in persistent handler state and assert that it remains zero, or distinguish expected protocol reverts from handler assertion failures so every assertion failure fails the campaign.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Every unexpected acceptance must produce a campaign failure; normal rejected calls may remain admissible exploration outcomes. Review that state rollback cannot erase the violation indicator.

findings.title: CREATE2 documentation overstates cross-chain address separation
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The factory documentation says a different chain yields a different account address. Its address calculation includes the factory, implementation and owner/policy salt, with no chain identifier. Equal addresses and inputs on two chains can therefore produce equal account addresses. Policy signatures remain chain-bound, so this is a documentation defect rather than a demonstrated signature replay flaw.
findings.impact_preconditions: Identical factory and implementation addresses and identical owner/policy inputs exist on multiple chains. Integrators rely on the stronger documentation claim.
findings.remediation: Document the actual CREATE2 inputs and distinguish account address derivation from the chain-bound EIP-712 signature domain.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: The documented prediction formula must match the implementation; cross-chain isolation claims must identify the particular domain-binding mechanism.

findings.title: Predeploy static checks do not have the claimed checksum parity
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The shell predeploy script claims the same static checks as the Forge scripts, but accepts any letter case in a 40-digit hexadecimal address. DeployBase requires the exact checksummed spelling. Without the optional Forge dry run, the preflight can print all checks passed before the deployment script rejects the configuration. The deployment checksum guard itself remains intact.
findings.impact_preconditions: An operator uses the static preflight with an address spelling rejected by DeployBase and does not enable the optional dry run.
findings.remediation: Share the checksum validation or describe the shell checks as format checks and make the remaining validation requirement explicit.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Preflight and deployment agree on accepted address spelling, or the preflight result precisely states the checks it omitted.

findings.title: NatSpec gate omits the policy router
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The NatSpec script describes coverage of production contracts but its explicit contract array omits GhostPayPolicyRouter. Existing documentation on that router does not repair the gate omission; later missing documentation in this production contract would be outside the stated gate.
findings.impact_preconditions: A documentation regression occurs only in GhostPayPolicyRouter and the project relies on this script for production-contract NatSpec coverage.
findings.remediation: Include GhostPayPolicyRouter and derive or reconcile the contract list against an authoritative production-contract inventory.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: All five first-party core production contracts are included in the stated documentation gate.

findings.title: Nonzero factory fees retain an immutable fee-token availability dependency
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: Fee collection occurs before account creation. Fee-token balance or allowance views that revert, or transfer behavior that violates the exact balance-delta checks, can prevent deployment to already-funded counterfactual policy addresses. The latest deployment script adds an explicit acknowledgement of this residual risk; it does not change the immutable factory. Ordinary clean transfer refusal can be waived under the factory conditions, so it would be inaccurate to say every blacklist or transfer refusal freezes deployment.
findings.impact_preconditions: FLAT_FEE is nonzero, an undeployed policy address already holds funds, and the chosen fee token becomes incompatible with the required views or deltas. This concerns supporting policy/direct integrations. The reviewed experimental web deployment helper rejects nonzero factory fees; this path is not a shipped lean-Pages feature.
findings.remediation: Prefer a zero-fee factory where fee-token independence is required. Any future fee-bearing design should preserve policy materialization when the fee token is unavailable, while retaining policy authorization. Existing immutable deployments require an explicit migration or funding restriction strategy.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Every offered funding path has a documented means to materialize and withdraw the resulting policy account under the stated token assumptions; an acknowledgement alone must not be represented as a technical fix.

findings.title: Reusable public policy hashes expose a payment correlation identifier
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The policy router exposes a public policy hash, and the factory computes that hash from destination, delay and limits root. Reusing those policy values retains the same public identifier even when one-time owner addresses differ. This supports correlation of payments sharing a policy; it does not alone prove a real-world identity or ownership.
findings.impact_preconditions: A receiver reuses the same policy values across scheme-2 payments. This is supporting policy functionality, not this specific field in the scheme-1 core payment path.
findings.remediation: Ensure privacy claims describe policy-level linkability. If policy-payment unlinkability is a requirement, review a protocol commitment design that does not publish a stable reused identifier.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Privacy documentation must match the identifiers actually emitted, and any revised commitment scheme must preserve payment-to-policy binding without an unintended stable public identifier.

findings.title: Policy asset restrictions can leave funded assets without an eligible withdrawal
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The policy router may send a native buffer into a policy account, while a nonzero limits root requires a matching asset leaf to authorize withdrawal. The payment builder receives the policy hash, not the policy contents needed to establish native-asset eligibility. A policy without an eligible native leaf can therefore retain an unusable native buffer. More generally, missing asset leaves and tokens incompatible with exact withdrawal deltas can strand direct deposits under the immutable policy. The native buffer is held by the policy account; it is not transaction gas delivered to the owner EOA.
findings.impact_preconditions: A restricted policy lacks the necessary asset eligibility, or funded token behavior violates withdrawal requirements. The native-buffer issue is conditional on selecting that payment option for such a policy.
findings.remediation: Require authenticated policy eligibility before offering native buffers or assets, explain the buffer purpose accurately, and reject unsupported asset funding paths in clients. Evaluate any future owner-authorized recovery design separately against the existing restrictions.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Every asset and buffer option offered by an integration is withdrawable under the authenticated policy and supported token behavior; recovery claims must account for immutable policy restrictions.

findings.title: Fee waiver assumptions do not distinguish sender-controlled transfer vetoes
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The factory allows fee-free deployment after a clean failed transfer when the prior fee balance and allowance are sufficient and observable state remains unchanged. A fee token with a payer-controlled sender hook can make that failure indistinguishable from the issuer-side refusal the waiver is intended to tolerate. The resulting risk is missed deployment-fee revenue, not policy ownership bypass or withdrawal of another owner's funds.
findings.impact_preconditions: An integration selects a nonzero factory fee and a fee token with suitable sender-controlled transfer behavior. The reviewed web helper only supports zero-fee factories.
findings.remediation: Explicitly qualify fee-token behavior, prefer zero fees where that qualification cannot be maintained, or redesign fee collection and liveness together.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Fee-token assumptions must address who can veto a transfer; accounting and availability expectations must remain consistent under all supported token behaviors.

findings.title: Immutable fee-recipient acceptance remains a payment availability dependency
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: Core and policy router transfers atomically deliver a nonzero fee to an immutable recipient. If that recipient cannot receive the relevant native or token payment, the transaction reverts. Token restrictions on the recipient or a native-rejecting recipient contract can therefore disable affected nonzero-fee payment paths. Atomic rollback prevents this from retaining the attempted payer funds in a partially completed payment.
findings.impact_preconditions: The computed fee is nonzero and the configured fee recipient becomes unable to receive the chosen asset. There is no mutable recipient repair path in these contracts.
findings.remediation: Qualify the recipient and assets at deployment, monitor the supported payment assumptions, and maintain clear client handling and deployment migration procedures. Any future resilience mechanism must preserve transparent fee routing.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Unavailable recipient/asset combinations are detected and surfaced before users rely on a successful payment; migration expectations reflect contract immutability.

findings.title: Sponsored sweeps retain relayer execution-cost and owner-state risks
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: Sweep execution calls token code and depends on owner state at execution time. A sponsor can incur transaction costs when token behavior, owner balance or allowance differs from the state it previously checked. The sweep signature binds the fee recipient and withdrawal destination, and unused token allowance alone does not authorize a new sweep. This is a protocol sponsorship assumption; this worker did not establish that a current relayer service lacks the relevant controls.
findings.impact_preconditions: A service sponsors transactions based on permissionless owner requests, and its supported token or execution policy permits costly failures or stale owner state.
findings.remediation: Apply supported-token qualification, fresh authorization/state checks, bounded gas expenditure and an explicit failed-transaction budget in the sponsoring service.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Sponsor economics must account for failed execution, and any production service claim must be checked in that service rather than inferred from the contract alone.

findings.title: Fee rounding and native-buffer exemptions are explicit economic semantics
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The percentage fee uses integer flooring, and the native buffer attached to a token payment is not included in that percentage fee. These are existing contract semantics rather than a newly identified authorization defect. Claims that all transmitted native value is charged would need to account for the buffer exemption and small-payment rounding.
findings.impact_preconditions: A product or economic claim assumes fees on all value, including native buffers or amounts that round below a fee unit.
findings.remediation: Align fee documentation, displays and revenue assumptions with the actual computation. Treat changes to the exemption as protocol changes.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Client explanations and accounting agree with the contract fee formula for each payment type.

findings.title: Announcement syntax does not by itself establish payment authenticity
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The router enforces the public-key encoding length and prefix and a structured metadata format; callers still choose assets and announcement inputs. Integrations must perform the remaining point, derivation, asset and actual-payment checks. The predecessor crypto review covered the relevant point-validation code. No current client spoofing path was established by this worker.
findings.impact_preconditions: An integration treats announcement appearance alone as authenticated payment or receiver ownership.
findings.remediation: Preserve full key/derivation checks, supported-asset policy and transaction-result verification at the receiving integration boundary.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Receiver credit and payment presentation must depend on verified payment facts, not only event shape or a candidate address.

findings.title: Main policy signing helper lacked the current canonical policy-only boundary
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: Main checked a caller-provided typed-data digest without restricting the domain and type structure to this package's policy structs, and read the caller digest again during signing. The release/latest implementation reconstructs the digest from validated canonical policy fields once and signs that local value. The inspected web withdrawal and cancel helpers construct their own typed data, so an externally reachable main-web path supplying arbitrary typed-data objects was not established.
findings.impact_preconditions: Historical exposure requires a caller able to supply an untrusted typed-data object to the secret-bearing library helper. The changed library boundary must not be presented as an established remote compromise of the web app.
findings.remediation: Retain the canonical policy-only reconstruction and one-time input capture on branches that ship this helper.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Only the exact supported domain, type and message fields reach the signer; subsequent mutation of caller-owned objects cannot alter the digest being signed.

findings.title: Main policy proofs lacked the current stored-field binding checks
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The historical library verified stored Merkle membership without all of the current recomputation checks tying token, limit and window fields to the stored leaf. Latest code adds that binding in proof retrieval and withdrawal construction. The on-chain account already recomputes and verifies the leaf, so this historical weakness supports client misplanning or rejected requests rather than an on-chain limit bypass.
findings.impact_preconditions: Untrusted or corrupted restored policy-tree data reaches historical client helpers.
findings.remediation: Retain stored-leaf recomputation and withdrawal-field binding when restoring policy data and building requests.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Every accepted proof has a leaf recomputed from its stated token, limit and window, and malformed stored data is rejected before signing.

findings.title: Main policy calldata decoder lacked current canonical and metadata checks
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The historical decoder parsed the expected method and bound the predicted account, while latest additionally requires canonical re-encoding, full ephemeral-point parsing and metadata consistency with payment asset and amount. These are strengthened decoder checks. Even the current decoder cannot establish that a separately supplied receiver policy is authentic; integrations must preserve that independent binding.
findings.impact_preconditions: Historical callers rely on this helper to validate untrusted payment calldata or treat successful decoding as broader payee authentication.
findings.remediation: Retain the latest canonical decoder and keep receiver-policy authentication explicit in the caller.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Accepted calldata is canonical and internally consistent, and successful decoding is not equated with authenticated receiver ownership.

findings.title: Main viewing-secret cleanup did not cover earlier validation failures
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The historical policy derivation helper copied the viewing secret before validations outside its cleanup region. The latest helper validates the nonsecret inputs first and protects the secret-copy lifetime. This is a best-effort memory-hygiene improvement in JavaScript; no remote secret-exfiltration path was established.
findings.impact_preconditions: A historical helper invocation fails validation after creating the temporary secret copy.
findings.remediation: Retain the latest ordering and ensure all secret-copy lifetimes enter guaranteed cleanup immediately.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Every local secret copy is covered by cleanup on successful and exceptional exits, with no stronger memory-erasure guarantee than the runtime can provide.

findings.title: Main Mythril output handling lacked the latest completeness evidence
findings.confidence: High in static source behavior; runtime not exercised
findings.description: The historical wrapper and compatibility launcher lacked the current per-run completeness telemetry and strict evidence checks. Latest code requires fresh exclusive telemetry, ready state, a single report and zero recorded exceptions/timeouts/errors, and records source/tool identity. These changes strengthen evidence that the requested bounded analysis completed; neither version constitutes proof that the contracts have no vulnerabilities. No analyzer was executed in this audit.
findings.impact_preconditions: A historical analysis result is treated as a complete successful run despite missing completeness evidence.
findings.remediation: Retain the latest fail-closed evidence path, strict parsing and source/tool identity checks; keep conclusions bounded to the actual analysis performed.
findings.non_operational_validation_criteria: Missing, duplicate, malformed, stale or incomplete analysis evidence cannot be presented as a successful completed security analysis.
